statements.text: But, then, AI can also be incredibly destructive. So the only defense that we're going to have against AI is AI. So are we developing that capability too? You have—AI can do good, but then you also know that AI can do bad, so you have to have the defensive AI to fight the bad AI.
statements.context: Member of Congress questioning CISA leadership at a House hearing on American cybersecurity.

statements.text: The other thing that I'm thinking about is artificial intelligence. It seems to me that artificial intelligence could go a long way in providing cybersecurity. I don't know who can answer this. Am I right or am I wrong on that?
statements.context: Rep. Gimenez poses a question to witnesses during a House hearing on growing the national cybersecurity talent pipeline.

statements.text: the danger of — of, you know, AI and military purposes.
statements.context: House hearing on U.S. leadership in critical and emerging technologies, during a Q&A exchange with a witness.

statements.text: So it all—now it means that we have to win the artificial intelligence battle. Or is this just going to be a race that's going to be forever?
statements.context: Remarks during a House hearing on DHS and CISA roles in securing artificial intelligence.

statements.text: So at the end of the day, do you think—this could all be elementary. I mean, it appears to me that what we're heading for is cyber attacks are going to be launched by artificial intelligence networks, and they're going to be guarded against by artificial intelligence networks and that it's who has the smartest artificial intelligence is going to win the race or is going to win out in that battle or war, et cetera. Would that be accurate?
statements.context: House Homeland Security Committee hearing on DHS and CISA roles in securing AI, where Rep. Gimenez questions witnesses about AI-driven cyber conflict.

statements.text: I'm going back to my apocalyptic view of this whole thing. [...] we're not wholly dependent on anything.
statements.context: House hearing on DHS and CISA roles in AI security, questioning agency witnesses about critical-infrastructure resilience.

statements.text: I guess I am a little bit more pessimistic knowing what is coming. I think we should be investing in a ways to defeat what is coming. Not what is here, what is coming. Because at the end, if what I am hearing is true, you won't be able to defeat it. The quantum computing attached to AI will be able to penetrate any system anytime.
statements.context: House hearing on operational technology in the water sector, where Rep. Gimenez closes his questioning by warning of future AI and quantum-computing threats.

statements.text: In the future, with AI and quantum, you are not going to need people. The computers will be unleashed against us. I don't care how many people you have, you are not going to be able to defend it.
statements.context: Verbatim remarks by Rep. Carlos Gimenez during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on securing operational technology in the water sector.

statements.text: AI will play an integrating role in Army capability modernization and transformation efforts.
statements.context: Written response from Secretary of the Army Christine Wormuth to a question submitted by Rep. Carlos Gimenez during a hearing on the Army's FY2025 budget request.

statements.text: So it is critical that we win the race and we always have the most intelligent artificial intelligence if that is the way we are going to go, and I think that is the way that we are going to go.
statements.context: House Armed Services Committee hearing on DOD technology acquisition, September 16, 2024.

statements.text: the nation that leads in AI would be better protected against a nation that's somewhat behind? The better your AI is, the better you're going to be at protecting yourself. The better you are at AI, I guess the better you are going to be at attacking your adversary. Is that correct?
statements.context: Remarks during a House hearing examining the global impact of a CrowdStrike software update outage.

statements.text: Yes. I mean, AI scares me and that's why we have to be on top. Because the only defense against AI in the future, I mean, if it gets totally mature and it just starts writing code, and you have to have AI on your side that writes the counter code just as fast as it's getting this code. So you're going to have this—you're going to have millions of attacks per day and you have to defend against millions of attacks per day because these things will just generate attack after attack after attack. Now, then you put that with quantum computing, now you really got a problem.
statements.context: House hearing on the CrowdStrike software outage, questioning a cybersecurity company representative about future AI-driven threats.

statements.text: If I can interrupt, will that mature into AI writing code that will be malicious in nature?
statements.context: Asked during a House hearing on the global impact of a faulty CrowdStrike software update.

statements.text: I know that we face significant threats now from the technology that we have right now, but right around the corner, if not already here, is AI. So some of the techniques that we use to mitigate current drones won't work on AI because they won't be piloted. They'll just be given a mission. [...] Do we have any capabilities to actually go kinetic, actually knock these things down either through, you know, some kind of a projectile or with high energy that fries the systems? Do we have any of that available anywhere?
statements.context: House Homeland Security Committee hearing on unmanned aerial systems threats and countermeasures.

statements.text: I believe that the artificial intelligence technology is a national security technology, much as any weapon system that we have, maybe even more important than any weapon system that we have. [...] Hopefully the artificial intelligence will be able to guard itself.
statements.context: House Homeland Security Committee hearing on global cyber threats, Representative Gimenez questioning witnesses on AI as a strategic national security asset.

statements.text: I think they are using that for their advantage and to try to put an anchor around our research into AI, because they understand how critical it is for us to win AI, for them to win AI, because, frankly, it is the future. [...] I actually believe it is a huge security risk for the United States for those large corporations and their intellectual property to be in China and actually cooperating with Chinese authorities.
statements.context: Speaking at a House hearing on Chinese economic espionage and subnational influence, the congressman questions witnesses about US corporations operating in China and the risk of AI intellectual property transfer.
